c.tagline: Red-tiled valleys beneath the Ávila, guarded and grand.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; agree on a price (often in USD) with the driver before departing.

emergency.note: 171 is the national emergency dispatch line covering police, fire, and ambulance; CICPC (investigative police) can also be reached directly for crime reporting. English-speaking operators are rare, so ask hotel staff for help if needed.

hood_landmark.Las Mercedes: Centro San Ignacio, Las Mercedes, Caracas
hood_landmark.El Rosal: Centro Financiero Confinanzas area, El Rosal, Caracas

avoid.reason: Avoid the hillside barrios entirely — Petare, Catia, 23 de Enero, El Valle and similar — where violent crime is severe even by day.
Even in safer Chacao, Altamira and Las Mercedes, phone snatching and express kidnappings occur — don't display valuables, use trusted drivers, and avoid the airport road after dark.

hood_desc: Leafy, upscale residential district with plazas, cafes and a Metro station; popular with business travelers and families wanting a quieter, well-guarded base.
Caracas's main dining and nightlife district, packed with restaurants, bars and shopping malls; suits visitors who want to be at the center of the action after dark.
A polished mid-town area of high-rises, embassies and international hotels near the CCCT mall; good for business travelers wanting a central, relatively calm location.
A compact financial and hotel district wedged between Chacaíto and Las Mercedes, walkable to bars and offices; suits travelers who prioritize convenience over sightseeing.
A historic, lively pedestrian boulevard near Plaza Venezuela with budget lodging and street life; suits budget travelers and those wanting a slice of everyday Caracas.

water.note: Tap water is unreliable and unsafe for visitors; drink bottled water.

transit.pay: Metro fares are paid with a rechargeable magnetic or contactless card sold and topped up at station booths; cash is not accepted directly at turnstiles. Buses, Metrobús and por puesto shared vans are paid in cash (bolívares, and increasingly USD) directly to the driver.
transit.hours: Metro runs roughly 5:30 AM to 11 PM daily with no all-night service; late-night travelers rely on taxis or ride-hailing apps.
transit.note: Fares are heavily subsidized and very cheap in USD terms, but overcrowding, occasional breakdowns and long queues are common.

airport.name: Simón Bolívar International Airport (CCS)
airport.drive: 35-60 min via the Autopista Caracas-La Guaira mountain highway, longer with traffic or checkpoints

transit.m: Aeroexpresos shuttle bus to Parque Central (~45 min)
Shared por puesto van to Gato Negro/Metro (~50 min)

tip.r: Some restaurants add a 10% service charge; if not included, a similar tip is appreciated but not obligatory.
